title: Reverse engineering: history, protocol analysis, and ethical limits

spans.text: Reverse engineering observes and documents how an existing device works. It can support repair, interoperability, migration, and debugging of equipment you own or are authorized to test.

Historical example: in the 1980s, companies building IBM-PC-compatible computers studied BIOS behavior and wrote independent implementations; clean-room practice separated observation from implementation. This illustrates interoperability, not blanket legal permission.

For your own sensor, start with its datasheet and public protocol. Use a logic analyzer on your own UART/I²C/SPI signals, document the byte layout, checksum, and units, then test a decoder. The sample parses a tiny frame from a device you control. For firmware research, confirm ownership and permission, record the exact version, preserve an original copy, and test only in a lab.

spans.title: Important safety and compatibility note
spans.text: Analyze only devices you own or are explicitly authorized to test. Do not use this lesson to bypass protections, extract others' data, or probe third-party networks. Copyright, patent, contract, and local laws vary.

visual_description: Add a wiring schematic and pin map showing board pins, VCC/GND, and signal direction; include a memory or task-state diagram where relevant.
